sum: Revenue jumped 27% and data center royalties doubled, but a post-midterm tech sell-off sent the stock down 13%
Arm Holdings just turned in the biggest quarter in its history. The stock then fell 13% the next day.

The chip designer reported fiscal second-quarter revenue of $1.44 billion for the period ending September 30, 2026, a 27% jump from a year earlier. It also laid out a long-range target that would turn its new chip-making venture into the core of the business: $15 billion in annual revenue from its Arm AGI CPU by 2031.
Wall Street was in no mood to celebrate. Shares slid in after-hours trading Wednesday, right after the report landed. The decline deepened Thursday, November 6, as a broad selloff hit tech stocks.
Arm is best known for licensing its power-efficient CPU architecture. Other companies pay for the blueprints, build the chips, and send Arm a cut of every unit sold.
That model produced two very different growth rates this quarter. Licensing and other revenue surged 50% to $773 million. Royalty revenue grew a more modest 8% to $670 million.
The gap matters. Licensing fees reflect new deals signed today, while royalties reflect chips actually shipping. This quarter, the upfront money outran the per-chip money by more than $100 million.

sum: Arm Holdings (ARM) reported results for the second quarter of fiscal 2027, ended September 30, after the U.S. market close on November 4. Revenue for the quarter was $1.443 billion, up 27% year-over-year, marking the fifth consecutive quarter of growth above 20% and a record high for the company's second fiscal quarter. However, net income calculated under U.S. generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) was just $130 million, down 45% year-over-year, with GAAP diluted earnings per share of $0.12 versus $0.22 a year earlier. Following the results, the company's shares fell more than 5% at one point after hours.
The report showed a clear divergence: revenue set a record driven by AI data centers and licensing, while profit was weighed down by one-time accounting factors and a high year-ago base.
Profit decline stems from one-time factors, operating metrics remain solid

Looking at net income alone, Arm's profitability appears to have deteriorated markedly. But the report also disclosed that the GAAP profit decline was mainly dragged down by two one-time factors: a $46.6 million fair value loss on publicly traded equity investments recognized in the quarter, and a $4.9 million net expected credit loss related to Arm China. More critically, the year-ago period included a $131 million pre-tax gain from the sale of the Artisan foundation IP business to Cadence, creating a high comparison base.

Excluding these factors, non-GAAP metrics reflecting core operations remained strong: non-GAAP net income of $566 million, up 36% year-over-year; non-GAAP diluted earnings per share of $0.52, up 33%; non-GAAP operating income of $638 million, with an operating margin of 44.2%, up 300 basis points year-over-year. GAAP operating income was $201 million, up 23%. Gross margins remained at extremely high levels, with GAAP gross margin of 97.1% and non-GAAP gross margin of 97.9%.

Changes on the expense side warrant attention. Non-GAAP research and development expenses were $547 million, up 17% year-over-year; non-GAAP operating expenses were $774 million, up 19%. CEO Rene Haas said on the earnings call that Arm is continuing to expand its engineering capabilities, investing in next-generation platforms, compute subsystems and the AGI CPU product line.

sum: Arm Holdings reported record fiscal first-quarter results on July 29, with revenue growing 22% to $1.29 billion, driven by surging data center demand and AGI CPU adoption. Despite beating earnings and issuing strong guidance, shares initially fell 8% due to high valuations exceeding 100x earnings and concerns over rising operating expenses. While AI-driven growth in Neoverse and Armv9 architectures justifies a premium, future royalty growth faces potential headwinds from smartphone market volatility. Investor sentiment remains tied to these long-term AI prospects, with the stock currently testing critical resistance levels near $280 amid a broader semiconductor rally.

TradingKey - On July 29, Arm Holdings (ARM) published their fiscal first quarter, and blew past every estimate. The stock fell 8% upon the news. It has since climbed with the broader chip stock rally to $273, but the initial reaction demonstrated the problem with Arm. Even with stellar quarterly numbers, shares may be fairly priced, and stock performance is negatively impacted by a hard beat.

The first quarter numbers emerged as an impressive 22% revenue increase, with the first quarter record numbers coming in at $1.29 billion. The guidance for the second quarter was expected to be low, but Arm published guidance above analyst estimates for the second quarter. The question is what all of that is worth.

Arm posted outstanding numbers across the board. Total revenue grew 22% year over year to $1.289 billion ($1.27 billion expected), marking a record for the first quarter. Royalty revenue also grew 22% year over year to $715 million, which was also a record for the first quarter. The data center was the most impressive segment with year over year royalty revenue growth more than doubling. This was a direct result of the cloud and AI providers adopting Arm's Neoverse technology.

Shipments of Neoverse have now amassed over 1.5 billion cores. Licensing revenue grew 23% to $574 million, while the annualized contract value (which measures the committed future revenue) grew by 13% to $1.732 billion. As Arm does not manufacture chips, their margins are higher, with a non-GAAP gross margin of 98.1%. Non-GAAP EPS grew 28% to $0.45, beating the $0.40 estimate, and Free Cash Flow was $665 million.

Jury Rules Against Arm Holdings (NASDAQ: ARM) In Qualcomm License Breach Case As Data-Center Security Deal Signals AI Ambitions
sum: A jury has determined that Arm Holdings (NASDAQ: ARM) violated its Architectural License Agreement with Qualcomm, and further concluded that the breach was intentional rather than incidental.
The finding that Arm deliberately acted to disrupt Qualcomm’s business adds a sharper edge to what might otherwise have been treated as a routine contractual dispute.

For a semiconductor company whose entire revenue model depends on licensing CPU and chip intellectual property to hardware makers and cloud providers, a jury verdict of this nature strikes at the core of how it operates.

Arm, which carries a market capitalization of roughly $224.6 billion, has been repositioning away from smartphone royalties and toward higher-margin AI and data-center compute as the next engine of growth.
That strategic shift makes the Qualcomm ruling particularly sensitive, given that major chip customers like Qualcomm also maintain relationships with rivals including Nvidia and Intel.

Analysts had already identified execution risk as Arm transitions from selling pure IP toward delivering more complete compute solutions, and the verdict may amplify those concerns among institutional investors.

Yet on the same day the jury delivered its ruling, Arm announced a partnership with Axiado to embed secure control modules directly into its AGI CPU server platform, targeting data center deployments.

sum: Chip technology supplier Arm Holdings breached a licensing agreement with Qualcomm and intentionally interfered with the chipmaker’s business relationship with Meta Platforms, a Delaware jury found on Tuesday, but awarded nominal damages of just $2.

Arm said that “despite Qualcomm’s pursuit of this case in an attempt to deprive Arm of billions of dollars under our license agreements, the jury’s verdict confirms that Arm operated in good faith under its technology license agreement and its award of only two dollars confirms the merit of Arm’s arguments in the case.”
The jury found Arm breached its obligation to provide software patches and tools for its designs. The jury found for Arm on five other breach allegations.

sum: CNBC's Jim Cramer on Tuesday urged investors to resist getting greedy when stocks go parabolic.

"Instead, I say go for the stairstep stocks. They won't seem to make you as money as fast as a stock running parabolic, but notice the word seem," the "Mad Money" host said. " Remember, you don't make money until you sell and the vast majority of people who are in a parabola never let go."

A parabolic move occurs when a stock's gains accelerate rapidly, often after a strong catalyst draws in momentum investors and pushes shares sharply higher. While those rallies can generate outsized returns, Cramer warned they often unravel just as quickly once sentiment turns.

Many stocks tied to artificial intelligence infrastructure and the data center buildout soared during the first half of the year before pulling back sharply in recent weeks. Shares of chipmaker Sandisk, for example, have plunged more than 50% from their June 25 record high after an enormous run dating back to last year. Cramer said that's why his Charitable Trust, the portfolio used by the CNBC Investing Club, trims positions when they've gone parabolic, rather than trying to call the exact top.
"I always advocate taking something off the table when a stock goes parabolic," he said.

He pointed to Arm Holdings and Corning as recent examples. The Club exited its Arm position on July 8 after just a few months of ownership. It took profits on multiple occasions in May and early June while the stock surged, before Cramer ultimately decided its swings were too volatile for his liking. Arm shares have fallen 44% from their June 18 record high. Meanwhile, the Club trimmed its Corning position multiple times in late June, locking in gains before the stock's momentum evaporated. Corning has tumbled more than 50% from its June 29 all-time high, including 12% on Tuesday despite reporting better-than-expected second-quarter results. The Club continues to own Corning shares and maintains an upbeat view of its long-term prospects.

Cramer cautioned investors against viewing those steep declines as automatic buying opportunities, arguing that once a parabolic rally breaks, selling pressure can persist long after the fundamentals remain intact.

Its expanding software ecosystem, deepening partnerships with hyperscalers and ambitious push into AI infrastructure continue to reinforce the company's long-term growth story.
ARM's Expanding Ecosystem Creates a Powerful Competitive Moat

ARM has built one of the semiconductor industry's strongest competitive advantages through a deeply interconnected ecosystem linking software developers and hardware manufacturers. This two-sided network has evolved into a durable competitive moat that becomes stronger as adoption continues to expand.

The company's architecture has become the preferred standard for device manufacturers because of its broad compatibility with leading operating systems, including Android, iOS, Windows and Linux. This extensive software support gives hardware manufacturers confidence that Arm-based processors will seamlessly run widely used applications, developer tools, and enterprise software across multiple computing environments.

The benefits extend equally to software developers. As more hardware companies adopt Arm's architecture, developers gain immediate access to an enormous installed base of devices, creating greater incentives to optimize applications for Arm-powered systems. Every additional hardware partner strengthens the software ecosystem, while broader software compatibility attracts even more hardware manufacturers.

This self-reinforcing cycle has helped ARM establish an exceptionally strong competitive position. The company's intellectual property now powers nearly every smartphone globally, creating significant barriers for competitors seeking to challenge its dominance in mobile CPU architecture.
